source_text: Τούτων ἤδη προδιηνυσμένων ἑπόμενον ἂν εἴη τὸν παιδαγωγὸν ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν τὸν βίον ἡμῖν τὸν ἀληθινὸν ὑποτυπώσασθαι καὶ τὸν ἐν Χριστῷ παιδαγωγῆσαι ἄνθρωπον. ἔστι δὲ ὁ χαρακτηρισμὸς οὐ φοβερὸς ἄγαν αὐτοῦ οὐδὲ ἔκλυτος κομιδῇ ὑπὸ χρηστότητος. ἐντέλλεται δὲ ἅμα καὶ χαρακτηρίζει τὰς ἐντολὰς ὡς ἡμᾶς αὐτὰς ἐκτελεῖν δύνασθαι. καί μοι δοκεῖ αὐτὸς οὗτος πλάσαι μὲν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐκ χοός, ἀναγεννῆσαι δὲ ὕδατι, αὐξῆσαι δὲ πνεύματι, παιδαγωγῆσαι δὲ ῥήματι, εἰς υἱοθεσίαν καὶ σωτηρίαν ἁγίαις ἐντολαῖς κατευθύνων, ἵνα δὴ τὸν γηγενῆ εἰς ἅγιον καὶ ἐπουράνιον μεταπλάσας ἐκ προσβάσεως ἄνθρωπον, ἐκείνην τὴν θεϊκὴν μάλιστα πληρώσῃ φωνήν· »ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ᾿ εἰκόνα καὶ καθ᾿ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμῶν.« καὶ δὴ γέγονεν ὁ Χριστὸς τοῦτο πλῆρες, ὅπερ εἴρηκεν ὁ θεός, ὁ δὲ ἄλλος ἄνθρωπος κατὰ μόνην νοεῖται τὴν εἰκόνα. ἡμεῖς δέ, ὦ παῖδες ἀγαθοῦ πατρός, ἀγαθοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ θρέμματα, πληρώσωμεν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός, ἀκούωμεν τοῦ λόγου καὶ τὸν σωτήριον ὄντως ἀναμαξώμεθα τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν βίον· ἐνθένδε ἤδη τὴν ἐπουράνιον μελετῶντες πολιτείαν, καθ᾿ ἣν ἐκθεούμεθα, τὸ ἀειθαλὲς εὐφροσύνης καὶ ἀκήρατον εὐωδίας ἐπαλειφώμεθα χρῖσμα, ἐναργὲς ὑπόδειγμα ἀφθαρσίας τὴν πολιτείαν ἔχοντες τοῦ κυρίου καὶ τὰ ἴχνη τοῦ θεοῦ διώκοντες· ᾧ μόνῳ προσήκει σκοπεῖν καὶ δὴ μέλει πῶς καὶ τίνα τρόπον ὑγιεινότερος ἂν ὁ τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίος γένοιτο. ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς αὐτάρκειαν τοῦ βίου καὶ ἀπεριττότητα ἔτι τε εὔζωνόν τε καὶ εὔλυτον ὁδοιπορικὴν ἑτοιμότητα εἰς ἀιδιότητα εὐζωΐας παρασκευάζει, αὐτὸν αὑτοῦ ἕκαστον ἡμῶν ταμιεῖον εἶναι διδάσκων. »μὴ γὰρ μεριμνᾶτε«, φησί, »περὶ τῆς αὔριον«, χρῆναι λέγων τὸν ἀπογεγραμμένον Χριστῷ αὐτάρκη καὶ αὐτοδιάκονον καὶ προσέτι ἐφήμερον ἐπαναιρεῖσθαι βίον. οὐ γὰρ ἐν πολέμῳ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν εἰρήνῃ παιδαγωγούμεθα. πολέμῳ μὲν οὖν πολλῆς δεῖ τῆς παρασκευῆς δαψιλείας τε χρῄζει ἡ τρυφή· εἰρήνη δὲ καὶ ἀγάπη, ἀφελεῖς καὶ ἀπράγμονες ἀδελφαί, οὐχ ὅπλων δέονται, οὐ παρασκευῆς ἀσώτου· λόγος ἐστὶν αὐταῖς ἡ τροφή, ὁ τὴν ἐνδεικτικὴν καὶ παιδευτικὴν ἡγεμονίαν κεκληρωμένος λόγος, παρ᾿ οὗ τὸ εὐτελές τε καὶ ἄτυφον καὶ τὸ ὅλον φιλελεύθερον καὶ φιλάνθρωπον φιλόκαλόν τε ἐκμανθάνομεν, ἑνὶ λόγῳ μετ᾿ οἰκειότητος ἀρετῆς ἐξομοιούμενοι τῷ θεῷ. ἀλλ᾿ ἐκπόνει καὶ μὴ ἀπόκαμνε· ἔσῃ γὰρ οἷος οὐκ ἐλπίζεις οὐδ᾿ εἰκάσαι δύναιο ἄν. ὡς δὲ ἔστι τις ἄλλη μὲν φιλοσόφων ἀγωγή, ἄλλη δὲ ῥητόρων, παλαιστῶν δὲ ἄλλη, οὕτως ἐστὶν γενναία διάθεσις φιλοκάλῳ προαιρέσει κατάλληλος ἐκ τῆς Χριστοῦ παιδαγωγίας περιγινομένη, καὶ τὰ τῆς ἐνεργείας πεπαιδευμέναι σεμναὶ διαπρέπουσιν πορεία καὶ κατάκλισις καὶ τροφὴ καὶ ὕπνος καὶ κοίτη καὶ δίαιτα καὶ ἡ λοιπὴ παιδεία· οὐ γὰρ ὑπέρτονος ἡ τοιάδε ἀγωγὴ τοῦ λόγου, ἀλλ᾿ εὔτονος. ταύτῃ οὖν καὶ σωτὴρ ὁ λόγος κέκληται, ὁ τὰ λογικὰ ταῦτα ἐξευρὼν ἀνθρώποις εἰς εὐαισθησίαν καὶ σωτηρίαν φάρμακα, ἐπιτηρῶν μὲν τὴν εὐκαιρίαν, ἐλέγχων δὲ τὴν βλάβην καὶ τὰς αἰτίας τῶν παθῶν διηγούμενος καὶ τὰς ῥίζας τῶν ἀλόγων ἐκκόπτων ἐπιθυμιῶν, παραγγέλλων μὲν ὧν ἀπέχεσθαι δεῖ, τὰς ἀντιδότους δὲ ἁπάσας τῆς σωτηρίας τοῖς νοσοῦσι προσφέρων· τοῦτο γὰρ τὸ μέγιστον καὶ βασιλικώτατον ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ, σῴζειν τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα. τῷ μὲν οὖν ἰατρῷ οὐδὲν πρὸς ὑγείαν συμβουλεύοντι ἄχθονται οἱ κάμνοντες, τῷ δὲ παιδαγωγῷ τῷ θείῳ πῶς οὐκ ἂν ὁμολογήσαιμεν τὴν μεγίστην χάριν μὴ σιωπῶντι μηδὲ παρενθυμουμένῳ τὰς εἰς ἀπώλειαν φερούσας ἀπειθείας, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταύτας διελέγχοντι καὶ τὰς ὁρμὰς τὰς εἰς αὐτὰς διατεινούσας ἀνακόπτοντι καὶ τὰς καθηκούσας πρὸς τὴν ὀρθὴν πολιτείαν ὑποθημοσύνας ἐκδιδάσκοντι; πλείστην ἄρα ὁμολογητέον χάριν αὐτῷ. τὸ γάρ τοι ζῷον τὸ λογικόν, τὸν ἄνθρωπον λέγω, ἄλλο τι φαμὲν ἢ θεάσασθαι τὸ θεῖον δεῖν; θεάσασθαι δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν φημὶ χρῆναι ζῆν τε ὡς ὑφηγεῖται ἡ ἀλήθεια, ἀγαμένους ὑπερφυῶς τόν τε παιδαγωγὸν αὐτὸν καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ, ὡς πρέποντα ἀλλήλοις ἐστὶ καὶ ἁρμόττοντα· καθ᾿ ἣν εἰκόνα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἁρμοσαμένους χρὴ σφᾶς αὐτοὺς πρὸς τὸν παιδαγωγόν, σύμφωνον τὸν λόγον ποιησαμένους τοῖς ἔργοις, τῷ ὄντι ζῆν.
pass_a_gloss: Having already gone through these things, it would be fitting for us to outline the true life, having been pedagogued by Jesus, and the man in Christ. For the characteristic of Him is not overly frightening, nor is it careless in gentleness. He both commands and characterizes the commandments, as if we are able to fulfill them ourselves. And it seems to me that He Himself formed man from the earth, regenerated him with water, increased him with spirit, pedagogued him with word, guiding him towards adoption and salvation with holy commandments, so that having changed the man from the ground into a holy and heavenly one, He might fulfill that divine phrase: 'Let us make man according to the image and likeness of us.' And Christ became the fulfillment of what God said, whereas the other man is considered only in the image. But we, O children of a good Father, nurslings of a good Pedagogue, let us fulfill the will of the Father, let us listen to the Word, and truly let us follow the life of our Savior; from here, already practicing the heavenly citizenship, according to which we are deified, let us be anointed with the chrism of eternal joy and unfading fragrance, having the evident example of incorruptibility, the citizenship of the Lord, and following the footsteps of God; to whom alone it is fitting to consider and to care how and in what way the life of men might become more healthy. But He also prepares for self-sufficiency of life and freedom from excess, and for a ready and easy journey towards eternity of well-being, teaching each of us to be the steward of himself. 'Do not be anxious', He says, 'about tomorrow', saying that the life recorded in Christ should be self-sufficient and self-serving and also daily. For we are pedagogued not in war, but in peace. War indeed requires much preparation and extravagance; but peace and love, unencumbered and untroubled sisters, do not need arms, nor do they need reckless preparation; their nourishment is the Word, the Word that has been entrusted with the indicative and pedagogical leadership, from which we learn what is humble and unassuming and whole and philanthropic and loving beauty, being conformed to God with one Word, in familiarity with virtue. But work and do not faint; for you will be such as you do not hope, nor can you imagine. Just as there is one kind of training for philosophers, another for orators, and another for athletes, so there is a noble disposition, suitable for a love of beauty, coming from the pedagogy of Christ; and the serious and dignified actions of energy are in harmony with the journey and rest and nourishment and sleep and bed and diet and the rest of the pedagogy. For this kind of training is not excessive, but suitable. Therefore, the Word is also called Savior, having found the rational medicines for men towards sensitivity and salvation, watching over the opportunity, reproving the harm and explaining the causes of the passions and cutting out the roots of irrational desires, commanding what one should abstain from, and offering all the antidotes of salvation to the sick; for this is the greatest and most kingly work of God, to save humanity. The patients do not resent the doctor who advises nothing for health; how then shall we not acknowledge the greatest gratitude to the divine Pedagogue, who does not keep silent, nor does He remind us of the disobediences that lead to destruction, but also reproves them and cuts off the impulses that lead to them, and teaches the submissions that lead to the right citizenship? We must therefore acknowledge the greatest gratitude to Him. For what else do we say the rational animal, I mean man, needs to do, except to behold the divine? And to behold the human nature, I say, one needs to live as truth leads, having taken the Pedagogue Himself and His commandments in a superhuman way, as is fitting and harmonious with each other; according to which image we also, having been harmonized with them, must be conformed to the Pedagogue, having made the Word harmonious with our deeds, to live in being.

pass_b_english: Since we have already worked through these matters, it is fitting for us to set out the true life that has been formed in us by our Pedagogue Jesus, and the man in Christ. His character is not overwhelmingly frightening, nor is it altogether relaxed through kindness. He both commands and gives shape to the commandments in such a way that we are able to carry them out. It seems to me that He Himself formed the man from earth, regenerated him with water, made him grow by the Spirit, and educated him by the Word, guiding him toward adoption and salvation with holy commandments, so that, having transformed the man from the ground into a holy and heavenly being, He might fulfill that divine utterance: "Let us make man according to our image and likeness" (Gen 1:26). Christ has become the full realization of what God spoke, whereas the other man is regarded only in the image. But we, children of a good Father, nurslings of a good Pedagogue, let us fulfill the Father's will, let us listen to the Word, and let us truly follow the saving life of our Savior. From this point on, as we practice the heavenly citizenship by which we are deified, let us anoint ourselves with the chrism of everlasting joy and imperishable fragrance, having the Lord's citizenship as a manifest example of incorruptibility and following the footsteps of God — to whom alone it belongs to consider and to care how and in what way the life of human beings might become healthier. He also prepares us for the self-sufficiency of life and for freedom from excess, and for a ready and easy journey toward an eternity of well-being, teaching each of us to be his own steward. "Do not be anxious about tomorrow," He says, declaring that the life enrolled in Christ must be self-sufficient and self-serving and also day-by-day. For we are educated not in war but in peace. War indeed demands great preparation, and luxury requires lavish outlay; but peace and love, unencumbered and untroubled sisters, need no arms and no wasteful preparation. Their nourishment is the Word, the Word entrusted with the indicative and pedagogical rule, from which we learn what is inexpensive and unpretentious, what is whole and philanthropic and loving of beauty, being conformed to God by one Word in familiarity with virtue. But work at it and do not grow weary; for you will become such as you do not hope, nor can you imagine. Just as there is one sort of training for philosophers, another for orators, and another for athletes, so a noble disposition, suited to a love of beauty, arises from the pedagogy of Christ; and the serious and dignified actions of the life are in harmony with journey and rest, food and sleep, bed and diet, and the rest of the education. For this sort of training is not overstrained but well-tempered. Therefore the Word is also called Savior, because He discovered rational medicines for human beings toward sensitivity and salvation, watching for the opportune moment, convicting of harm, explaining the causes of the passions, cutting out the roots of irrational desires, commanding what must be avoided, and offering all the antidotes of salvation to the sick — for this is the greatest and most kingly work of God, to save humanity. Patients do not resent the physician who advises nothing for their health; how then shall we not acknowledge the greatest gratitude to the divine Pedagogue, who does not keep silent nor pass over the disobediences that lead to destruction, but convicts them, severs the impulses that stretch toward them, and teaches the submissions that lead to the right citizenship? We must therefore acknowledge the greatest gratitude to Him. For what else do we say the rational animal — I mean the human being — needs, except to behold the divine? And to behold human nature, I say, one must live as truth guides, having embraced the Pedagogue Himself and His commandments in a superhuman way, as is fitting and harmonious with each other; according to that image we also, having been harmonized with them, must conform ourselves to the Pedagogue, making the Word harmonious with our deeds, to live in being.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex theological descriptions of the Pedagogue's work and the distinction between the 'other man' and Christ. Scripture citations (Genesis 1:26) are correctly identified and added to the English text as required. The translation of 'τῷ ὄντι ζῆν' as 'to live in being' is a faithful rendering of the Greek participle/substantive construction.
